labels.modelNote: How this maps to a real model

actions.incomplete: Complete the three key activities first

page1.title: Some clues help more
page1.subtitle: All the tokens are visible, but they do not all help equally with the same question.
page1.question: Do all visible words help equally?
page1.intro: Lesson 2 showed which tokens are available. Now we can ask which of those visible tokens give the strongest clues for the current task.
page1.target: What is likely to be sleeping?
page1.analogy: Like looking for the best clues in a sentence.
page1.action: Tap the two tokens that help most.
page1.tryAgain: Look for the thing that slept and the action it performed.
page1.takeaway: For one task, some visible tokens can provide stronger clues than others.
page1.bridge: But the best clue can change when the task changes.

page2.title: The task changes the clues
page2.subtitle: The same sentence can create different useful connections.
page2.question: Is a word always equally helpful?
page2.intro: Keep the sentence the same. Change what we are trying to find, then watch the spotlight move to a different pair of tokens.
page2.takeaway: Helpful clues depend on what is being processed at that moment.
page2.modelNote: This classroom question helps us picture changing token relationships. A real language model performs numerical calculations between token representations.

page3.title: Clues can work together
page3.subtitle: More than one earlier token can contribute at the same time.
page3.question: Can several earlier tokens help together?
page3.intro: Follow three useful clues from the same sentence. Each one adds information to the relationship we are exploring.
page3.target: Why did Maya put on her coat?
page3.takeaway: Several earlier tokens can contribute to the current token representation.
page3.technicalNote: In transformer models, this kind of relationship is often described using attention. The model does not investigate like a human detective.
page3.bridge: The position of those clues also matters.

page4.title: Order changes relationships
page4.subtitle: The same words can describe a different event when their positions change.
page4.question: Why is a list of words not enough?
page4.intro: Both sentences contain the same main words. Follow their positions and decide who performs the action in each one.
page4.chooseActor: Choose who is doing the chasing
page4.tryAgain: Follow the tokens from left to right and check who appears before “chased”.
page4.takeaway: Order information helps the model distinguish different relationships between tokens.
page4.bridge: Now try finding helpful clues yourself.

page5.title: Find the helpful clues
page5.subtitle: Use the spotlight idea on reviewed classroom examples.
page5.question: Which visible tokens give the useful clues?
page5.intro: Select the clue blocks that best support the current classroom question. These examples help us picture token relationships; there may be other reasonable clues in real language.
page5.exampleA: Which clues help us understand where the nest is?
page5.exampleB: Which clues suggest rain may come?
page5.retry: Choose only the clues that most directly support this classroom question. You can try as many times as you like.
page5.explanationA: “high” and “tree” directly help locate the nest in this reviewed example.
page5.explanationB: “umbrella” and “dark clouds” are useful classroom clues that rain may come.
page5.boundary: A real model learns numerical relationships between tokens. This activity uses reviewed examples to help you picture the idea.
page5.takeaway: The model can connect the current token with useful information elsewhere in its context.
page5.bridge: Put the full clue-finding journey together.

page6.title: Your clue-finding discovery
page6.subtitle: Follow the route from visible context toward the next prediction step.
page6.question: How do helpful clues move the process forward?
page6.intro: The context window makes tokens available. Numerical relationships then combine useful information before prediction begins.
page6.cluesNote: Some provide stronger clues for this step.
page6.nextNote: The next lesson opens this step.
page6.point1: A context window contains the tokens currently available.
page6.point2: Some tokens provide stronger clues for the current step.
page6.point5: These connections help prepare the model to predict what may come next.
page6.accuracy: The model does not highlight words like a person. Transformer models use numerical calculations to combine information between token representations.
page6.next: After helpful context has been combined, the model can compare possible next tokens.
